Our theory allows for $\varepsilon$ to be different from $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}$; cf Theorem 4.2. In our numerical experiments in Section 2 we consider $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}$ to focus on other relevant quantities, namely $\psi_1$, $\psi_2$ on adversarial risk.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: We use $O_d(\cdot)$, $o_d(\cdot)$ to denote the standard big-O and little-o notation, where we stress the asymptotic variable $d$. Likewise, we use $O_{d,\mathbb P}$ and $o_{d,\mathbb P}$ to indicate asymptotic behavior in probability. Specifically, $f(d)=O_{d,\mathbb P}(g(d))$ if for any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $C_\varepsilon>0$ and large enough $d_\varepsilon$ such that $P(|f(d)/g(d)|>C_\varepsilon)\leq\varepsilon$, for all $d\geq d_\varepsilon$. Similarly, $f(d)=o_{d,\mathbb P}(g(d))$ if $f(d)/g(d)$ converges to zero in probability. We write $f(d)\approx g(d)$ as $d\to\infty$, when $f(d)-g(d)\to0$, in probability.
auxiliary_passages.resolution: The limit variable is d with dimensions growing as specified in the separate proportional-growth passage. A difference tending to zero is distinct from ratio convergence.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
For a matrix $\boldsymbol A$, we denote by $\|\boldsymbol A\|$ its operator norm, $\|\boldsymbol A\|_F=(\sum_{ij}A_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$ the Frobenius norm of $\boldsymbol A$. For an integer $n$, we use the shorthand $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$.

Finally, the indicator function is denoted by $\mathbb I(\cdot)$ – i.e., $\mathbb I(A)=1$ only if the event $A$ holds true, and otherwise $\mathbb I(A)=0$.

unresolved_source_conventions.detail: Part (a) defines nu with a superscript star; (4.6) uses nu with a subscript star, without an explicit sentence equating that symbol to the root evaluated at the saddle point. That evaluation is the apparent intended reading, but original notation is preserved and the distinction is recorded.

The optimization domain permits zero alpha, beta, tau_g and tau_q, but the objective and root equation divide by these quantities. No boundary extension or extended-real convention is given in the inspected main-text statement. The domain is not silently restricted to strict positivity.

No domain for nu is stated in the root assertion. The objective multiplies a root-dependent term by an indicator threshold, but no separate definition is supplied for inactive branches or zero denominators. A nonnegative-root restriction or zero-root fallback is not added.

The source gives i.i.d. pairs, Gaussian x marginals and Gaussian xi marginals, but does not explicitly write xi independent of x in the model statement. Independent additive Gaussian noise is the conventional intended model; the missing explicit independence is recorded rather than inserted into the source quotation.

The surrogate Gaussian u is explicitly independent of x; its independence from response noise and W is not separately stated in the defining sentence. The sample uses one shared W. The audit does not replace the conditional-on-W interpretation with unconditional independence of all feature vectors.

Theorem 6.9 does not cite Assumption 1. Section 6 explicitly reiterates proportional n,d,N growth, but not the signal norm tending to one. The graph includes the repeated dimensional convention and records the unstated signal-regime scope; it does not silently impose the stronger normalization merely because the theorem is used to prove Theorem 4.2.

The printed assertion that sigma(w_i^T x) has unit variance conflicts with the shifted-ReLU definition. The Gaussian decomposition coefficients are retained as stated, and sigma is not replaced by its standardized nonlinear component.
The main text defines S by a complete real formula and refers to Lemma F.2 for further transform details. The appendix is not consulted and no additional convention from it is assumed.

The scalar beta in the saddle problem is distinct from the bold signal vector beta in data model (2.1). Scalar sigma squared in Theorem 4.2 is distinct from the activation function sigma. The scalar lambda inside the supremum of (4.5) is distinct from the positive regularization lambda in Theorem 6.9.

The limit c has no separately printed quantifier or range, and lambda,lambda_s,lambda_w are stated only to be positive. Treating c as a deterministic finite real limit and penalties as fixed is conventional context; the theorem does not explicitly describe a growing/diminishing penalty regime.

The general adversarial-risk definition uses max for an arbitrary predictive model and nonnegative loss, without general regularity guaranteeing attainment. The specialized shifted-ReLU squared loss is continuous on a compact perturbation ball. The robust ERM uses an argmin without a general tie-selection convention; no tie rule is invented.
